title: The Stave, Clefs and Note Names

blocks.md:
- Identify the five lines and four spaces of a stave and explain what they are for
- Name and find the notes on the treble clef stave and on the bass clef stave
- Locate middle C on the piano and explain how it links the treble and bass clef staves
blocks.label: In this lesson

blocks.md:
When we write music down, we need a way to show two things at once: **which note to play** and **how high or low it sounds**. We do that with something called a **stave** (also called a **staff**).

A stave is simply **five horizontal lines stacked on top of each other**. That is all it is. Think of it like a ladder for the pitch of the notes.
**Stave**: five horizontal lines used to show musical pitch. Pitch means how high or low a note sounds.

Look at the stave below. Notice that between every two lines there is a gap. Those gaps are called **spaces**. Count the spaces too: there are exactly four of them and notes can occupy these spaces too.

blocks.caption: A blank stave with five lines and four spaces.

blocks.md:
Every note you read will sit in one of these two places:

- **On a line**, meaning the line runs right through the middle of the note.
- **In a space**, meaning the note sits between two lines.
The first note below sits **on** a line. The second note sits **in** a space. Notice how different the positions look. This difference tells you which note to play.
blocks.title: Lines and spaces side by side

blocks.caption: E sits on a line. F sits in the space just above it. Both are in the treble clef, which you will meet in the next section.

blocks.md:
Now here is the most important rule of the stave:

**Higher up on the stave means a higher-sounding note. Lower down means a lower-sounding note.**

This makes the stave very logical. As notes climb up the lines and spaces, the pitch climbs too.
Imagine the stave as a hill. Notes at the bottom of the hill sound low and deep. Notes at the top sound high and bright. Your eye and your ear follow the same direction.
Listen to three notes, one low, one in the middle, and one high. Notice how the sound rises as the note moves up the stave.

blocks.label: Low, middle, and high notes: hear the pitch rising

blocks.abc:
X:1
L:1/4
K:C
C, C c
blocks.caption: Three C notes at different heights on the stave. Lower positions sound lower. Higher positions sound higher.

blocks.label: The same three notes on the keyboard: low C, middle C, high C

items.prompt: How many lines does a stave have?
items.explain: A stave always has exactly five horizontal lines. Between those five lines there are four spaces.

items.prompt: You see two notes written on a stave. One note is higher up on the stave than the other. What does that tell you?
items.explain: Position on the stave shows pitch. Higher up on the stave always means a higher-sounding note. Duration, volume, and which hand to use are shown in other ways.
options: The higher note is longer in duration.
The higher note has a higher pitch.
The higher note is played with the left hand.

items.prompt: A note can sit either on a line or in a space on the stave.
items.explain: Correct. Every note is placed either directly on one of the five lines (the line runs through the note head) or in one of the four spaces between the lines.

blocks.title: Check your understanding: What Is a Stave?

blocks.md: A full-size piano has 88 keys. Middle C is the C note closest to the **middle** of that keyboard. It sits just left of centre, and it is the most important landmark note on the whole instrument. Once you can find it without thinking, every other note becomes easier to locate.
Look for a group of **two black keys**. The white key immediately to the left of those two black keys is always a C. The C that is closest to the centre of your keyboard is middle C.

blocks.label: Middle C on the keyboard

blocks.md: Go to your piano or keyboard right now. Find the group of two black keys nearest the middle of the keyboard. Press the white key just to the left of them. That is middle C.

blocks.label: Middle C

blocks.md:
Look at a blank stave and you will see five horizontal lines. On their own, those lines mean nothing. You need a symbol at the very start to tell you which note lives on which line or space. That symbol is called a **clef**.

A clef is simply a label for the stave. It says: "Here is where a specific note sits, and every other note is measured from there."
The clef you will meet first is the **treble clef**. It is also called the **G clef**, and in a moment you will see exactly why.

blocks.caption: A treble clef sitting at the start of a stave. Notice the large, curling symbol on the left.

blocks.md: Look closely at the shape of the treble clef. It has a long, sweeping curl that wraps around one of the five lines. That line is the **second line from the bottom** of the stave. The curl shows us that the line is the note **G** (specifically, the G just above the middle of the piano). Because it shows us the note G, the treble clef is called the G clef.
**The treble clef anchors the second line from the bottom as the note G.** Every other note on a treble stave can be found by counting up or down from that G.

blocks.caption: This note sits on the second line from the bottom of the treble stave. That line is G, fixed there by the treble clef's curl.

blocks.md: Here is what that G sounds like on a real piano. It is the G above middle C, and it sits comfortably in the upper-middle part of the keyboard.

blocks.label: G above middle C (the note the treble clef anchors)
G4: the note anchored by the treble clef's curl

blocks.md: The treble clef is used for **higher-pitched notes (and instruments)**. When you sit at the piano and use your **right hand**, you are almost always reading from a treble clef stave. Melodies, high accompaniment parts, and most of what the right hand plays live here.
Handy for your memory: the word **treble** itself means "high" or "upper", the same word used in "treble" voices in a choir.
Below are three notes written on a treble stave. One of them is sitting exactly on the second line from the bottom, which means it is G.
blocks.title: Spotting the anchor note G on the stave

blocks.abc:
X:1
L:1/4
K:C
| E G B2
blocks.caption: Three notes on the treble stave. The middle note (G) sits on the second line from the bottom, the line the treble clef anchors.

blocks.label: E, G, B: three notes on the treble stave

blocks.md: Sit at your piano and find the G above middle C on the keys (the keyboard diagram above shows you where it is). This is the note the treble clef is built around.

items.prompt: What is the purpose of a clef on a stave?
items.explain: A clef is a symbol placed at the start of a stave to identify which note each line and space stands for. Without it, the five lines have no meaning.
options: It tells you how fast to play the music.
It tells you which note each line and space represents.
It tells you how many beats are in a bar.
It tells you how loud to play.

items.prompt: The treble clef is also called the G clef. Why?
items.explain: The treble clef's distinctive curl wraps around the second line from the bottom of the stave. That act of "pointing to" the line fixes it as the note G, which is why it is called the G clef.
options: Because it was invented by a musician whose name started with G.
Because its curl wraps around the second line from the bottom, fixing that line as the note G.
Because it is only used for notes that sound like G.
Because G is always written at the top of the stave in treble clef.

items.prompt: The treble clef is used for higher-pitched notes and is what the right hand usually reads.
items.explain: Correct. The treble clef covers the higher part of the piano's range. When you play with your right hand, you are almost always reading from a treble clef stave.

blocks.title: Check your understanding: Meet the Treble Clef

blocks.md: The treble clef sits on a stave (the set of five horizontal lines used to write music). It has five lines and four spaces. Every single line and every single space has a letter name, A through to G. Once you know these names, you can read any note written in the treble clef.

Count the five lines from the bottom line upward. The notes sitting on those lines are, from bottom to top:

1. Bottom line: **E**
2. Second line: **G**
3. Middle line: **B**
4. Fourth line: **D**
5. Top line: **F**

**Memory phrase for the line notes:** Every Good Boy Deserves Fun

The first letter of each word gives you the note: **E, G, B, D, F**, from the bottom line to the top line.

blocks.abc:
X:1
L:1/4
K:C
E G B d f
blocks.caption: The five line notes of the treble clef, from bottom (E) to top (F). Each note sits directly on a line.

blocks.md:
Now look at the four spaces between the lines. The notes sitting inside those spaces are, from the bottom space upward:

1. Bottom space: **F**
2. Second space: **A**
3. Third space: **C**
4. Top space: **E**
**Memory phrase for the space notes:** The four space notes spell the word **FACE**. F, A, C, E, from the bottom space to the top space.

blocks.abc:
X:1
L:1/4
K:C
F A c e
blocks.caption: The four space notes of the treble clef, from bottom (F) to top (E). Each note sits inside a gap between two lines.

blocks.md: Put the line notes and space notes together and you get a smooth step-by-step ladder from E up to F, covering all nine notes: E, F, G, A, B, C, D, E, F. On the stave, that looks like this.

blocks.abc:
X:1
L:1/4
K:C
E F G A B c d e f
blocks.caption: All nine treble clef notes in order, stepping upward: E, F, G, A, B, C, D, E, F.

blocks.text: Find These Notes on the Piano

blocks.md: Let's connect the stave to real keys. First, find middle C. It is the C closest to the middle of your piano. Now move one white key to the right. That note is **D**. Move one more white key to the right. You are now on **E**, the very first note of the treble clef stave. This is the E just above middle C, and musicians call it E4 in scientific pitch naming.

blocks.label: E above middle C, your treble clef starting point
Listen: E above middle C (the bottom line of the treble clef)

blocks.md: Now let's walk up one white key at a time from that E, naming each note as we go. The notes match the ladder you saw on the stave above.

blocks.label: The nine treble clef notes on the keys: E, F, G, A, B, C, D, E, F
Listen: all nine treble clef notes stepping upward, E to F

blocks.md:
Sit at your piano and place your right hand with your thumb on E4 (two white keys above middle C).

1. Play each white key slowly, moving upward one at a time.
2. Say the note name out loud as you play it: E, F, G, A, B, C, D, E, F.
3. Try follow the notation above to get familiar with reading the notation while playing
4. Repeat two or three times until the names feel natural.
Do not rush. Playing slowly and saying each name aloud is far more useful than playing quickly and guessing. Your brain needs to hear the name and feel the key at the same time.

Using the mnemonics is a great way to get you started finding notes. However, a faster approach is to use **landmark notes**. These are a small set of notes you learn to recognise on sight, straight away, without counting.

The three most useful landmarks in the treble clef are:

- **Middle C** sits just below the stave, on its own short line called a ledger line.
- **G** sits on the second line from the bottom. This is the line the treble clef curl wraps around, so it is sometimes called the G clef.
- **C** in the third space on the stave and is the next C above middle C.

Once you know those landmarks, you can find any nearby note by moving just one or two steps up or down. For example, suppose you see a note on the **first space from the bottom**. You know the bottom line is E. One step up from E is F, and a space is one step up. So the note is **F**.

Suppose you see a note in the **third line from the bottom**. You know the second line is G. Count up from G: the second space is A and the third line is B so that note is **B**.

With practice you will recognise landmarks instantly, and nearby notes will follow quickly.
blocks.title: Spotting a note on the stave

items.prompt: What note sits on the middle line (third line from the bottom) of the treble clef?
items.explain: The five line notes from bottom to top are E, G, B, D, F (Every Good Boy Deserves Fun). The third line from the bottom is B.

items.prompt: The four space notes of the treble clef spell a word. What is that word?
items.explain: The four space notes from bottom to top are F, A, C, E, which spell the word FACE. This is the key memory trick for the space notes.

items.prompt: The note on the bottom line of the treble clef is the E just above middle C on the piano.
items.explain: Correct. The bottom line of the treble clef is E4, which is the E immediately above middle C (C4) on the keyboard. It is two white keys to the right of middle C.

blocks.md:
You have just met the treble clef, which handles higher-pitched notes. Now on to its partner: the **bass clef**.

The bass clef covers the **lower-pitched notes** on the piano. As a general rule, your **left hand reads the bass clef**. While your right hand plays the notes written on the treble stave, your left hand plays the notes written on the bass stave.
**Reminder:** A stave is five horizontal lines used to write music on. Each line and each gap between lines represents a different note. You met the stave in Section 1.

blocks.text: What Does the Bass Clef Look Like?

blocks.md:
The bass clef is also called the **F clef**. It has two parts that make it easy to spot:

1. A curved symbol that looks a little like a backwards letter C with a thick dot
2. Two smaller dots, sitting around the fourth line from the bottom

Those two dots are not just decoration. They **point to the fourth line from the bottom of the stave**, and that line is fixed as the note **F**. That is exactly why the bass clef has another name: the F clef.

blocks.caption: The bass clef on a stave. The two dots sit above and below the fourth line from the bottom, marking that line as the note F.

blocks.md: **Remember it this way:** the two dots of the bass clef act like a sign post wrapped around the note F.

The bass clef lives in a lower part of the piano than the treble clef. To get a feel for this, compare these two F notes. The first is a high F, in the treble range. The second is a low F, in the bass range. Listen to how much deeper the bass note sounds.

blocks.label: A high F (treble range)
F3: the note the bass clef symbol wraps around

blocks.md: That deep, warm sound is the world the bass clef describes. It is the sound of your left hand moving in the lower half of the keyboard.

The F that the bass clef fixes is F3, which sits to the left of middle C on the keyboard. Find it now by looking for a group of three black keys. The white key directly to the left of the first black key in that group is F.

blocks.label: F3: the note named by the bass clef's two dots
F3: the anchor note of the bass clef

blocks.md:
- Also called: the **F clef**
- Used for: **lower-pitched notes**
- Typically read by: the **left hand**
- Anchor note: the **fourth line from the bottom** of the stave is fixed as **F**
- The two dots sit above and below that fourth line as a constant reminder
blocks.title: The Bass Clef at a Glance

blocks.md: Play a few notes in the lower area of the piano and just listen to the deep, rich sound. Then find F3 using the guide above: look for the first group of three black keys to the left of middle C, and play the white key just to the left of that group. That note, F3, is the anchor of everything the bass clef will show you.

items.prompt: The bass clef is sometimes called the F clef. Why does it have that name?
items.explain: The two dots of the bass clef pinpoint the fourth line from the bottom of the stave and declare it to be the note F. That is why the clef earned the nickname 'the F clef'.
options: Because it was invented by a composer whose name began with F
Because its two dots fix the fourth line from the bottom of the stave as the note F
Because it only uses the note F
Because F stands for 'full', meaning it covers all notes

items.prompt: The bass clef is used for higher-pitched notes, and is usually read by the right hand.
items.explain: The bass clef covers lower-pitched notes and is normally read by the left hand. The treble clef handles higher-pitched notes for the right hand.

items.prompt: On the bass clef stave, where exactly do the two dots sit?
items.explain: The two dots of the bass clef sit just above and just below the fourth line from the bottom, squeezing that line between them to mark it as F.
options: Above and below the first line from the bottom
Above and below the middle (third) line
Above and below the fourth line from the bottom
Above and below the top line

blocks.title: Check Your Understanding: Meet the Bass Clef

blocks.md:
The bass clef has five lines and four spaces, just like the treble clef. Each line and each space has a letter name.

Your job in this section is to learn which line or space belongs to which letter.

The lines in the bass clef are counted from the bottom upwards. The note sitting on each line, from bottom to top, is:

- Line 1 (bottom): **G**
- Line 2: **B**
- Line 3 (middle): **D**
- Line 4: **F**
- Line 5 (top): **A**

**Memory phrase for the bass clef lines:**

**G B D F A** = **Good Boys Deserve Fun Always**

Start at the bottom line and say one word per line as you go up.

blocks.abc:
X:1
L:1/4
K:none clef=bass
G,, B,, D, F, A,
blocks.caption: The five bass clef line notes, from bottom to top: G, B, D, F, A. Each note sits directly on a line.

blocks.md:
The spaces are also counted from the bottom upwards. The note sitting in each space, from bottom to top, is:

- Space 1 (lowest): **A**
- Space 2: **C**
- Space 3: **E**
- Space 4 (highest): **G**

**Memory phrase for the bass clef spaces:**

**A C E G** = **All Cows Eat Grass**

Start at the lowest space and say one word per space as you go up.

blocks.abc:
X:1
L:1/4
K:none clef=bass
A,, C, E, G,
blocks.caption: The four bass clef space notes, from bottom to top: A, C, E, G. Each note sits in the gap between two lines.

blocks.md: Notice how the lines and spaces interlock neatly. Reading upwards from the bottom, the full sequence goes: G (line), A (space), B (line), C (space), D (line), E (space), F (line), G (space), A (line). That is simply the musical alphabet climbing step by step.

blocks.abc:
X:1
L:1/4
K:C clef=bass
G,, A,, B,, C, D, E, F, G, A,
blocks.caption: All nine bass clef notes in order, from G on the bottom line up to A on the top line: G, A, B, C, D, E, F, G, A.

blocks.text: Finding These Notes on the Piano

blocks.md:
Let's connect what you see on the stave to what you play on the keys. The bass clef covers the notes to the left of middle C on the piano. We will start with G, the bottom line of the bass clef.

To find this G, sit at the piano and locate the group of three black keys just below middle C. The white key just below the lowest of those three black keys is F (F3). Now find the next group of three black notes below that F and find another F (F2). One note above the F is G, the lowest line on the stave.

blocks.label: G below middle C: the bottom line of the bass clef
Bottom line of the bass clef: G below middle C

blocks.md: Now let's hear all nine notes climbing up the bass stave, from that G all the way to the A on the top line. Listen for how the sound rises smoothly, one step at a time and try follow the notes on the stave above.

blocks.label: All bass clef notes climbing upward: G, A, B, C, D, E, F, G, A
All nine bass clef notes: G, A, B, C, D, E, F, G, A

blocks.md:
Sit at the piano and find the bottom G on the stave with your left hand.

1. Play G and say its name aloud.
2. Move up one white key at a time, saying the letter name of each note as you go: G, A, B, C, D, E, F, G, A.
3. Repeat the climb two or three times until the names feel natural under your fingers.
If you lose track of where you are, just come back to G and start again. Returning to a familiar starting point is a great habit at any level.

A common mix-up: the top line of the bass clef is **A**, and the top space is **G**. In other words, A sits above G here, which is the opposite of what some learners expect. The phrase "All Cows Eat **Grass**" ends on G (the top space), and the A on the top line sits just above it.

items.prompt: Which note sits on the third line (middle line) of the bass clef?
items.explain: The three middle lines of the bass clef, counting from the bottom, are G, B, and D. The third line is D. The phrase 'Good Boys Deserve Fun Always' gives you G, B, D, F, A from bottom to top.

items.prompt: The phrase 'All Cows Eat Grass' helps you remember the bass clef space notes. What is the note in the second space from the bottom?
items.explain: The space notes from bottom to top are A, C, E, G. 'All Cows Eat Grass' maps to A, C, E, G. The second space is C, matching the word 'Cows'.

items.prompt: The note on the top line of the bass clef is G.
items.explain: The top line of the bass clef is A, not G. G sits in the top space, just below the top line. The phrase 'Good Boys Deserve Fun Always' ends with A on the top line.

blocks.title: Check Your Understanding: Bass Clef Note Names

blocks.text: Middle C: The Note That Joins Them

blocks.md: You have now met the treble clef and the bass clef. Each one has its own five lines and its own note names. But one note belongs to both worlds: **middle C**, the keyboard landmark you found at the very start. Now let's see how that single key is written in each clef, and why it is the note that joins them.

blocks.text: Middle C in the Treble Clef

blocks.md: Middle C is quite a low note for the treble clef. It does not fit inside the five main lines of the treble stave. Instead, it sits **just below** the bottom line, resting on its own tiny extra line.

That tiny extra line has a name. It is called a **ledger line**. A ledger line is a short extra line added above or below a stave when a note falls outside the five main lines. Think of it as a mini stave extension, just long enough for one note.

blocks.abc:
X:1
L:1/4
K:C clef=treble
M:none
C4
blocks.caption: Middle C in the treble clef. It sits on a short extra line called a ledger line, just below the five main lines of the stave.

blocks.md: Notice that the note head sits **on** the ledger line, the way any note sits on one of the five main lines. The ledger line passes neatly through the middle of the note head.

blocks.text: Middle C in the Bass Clef

blocks.md: Middle C is equally a high note for the bass clef. It does not fit inside the five main lines of the bass stave either. This time it sits **just above** the top line, again on its own ledger line.

blocks.caption: Middle C written in the bass clef. It sits on a ledger line just above the stave.

blocks.md: Both of these written notes, the one below the treble stave and the one above the bass stave, are **exactly the same pitch**. They are the same key on your piano. The notation is different because each clef has its own frame, but the sound is identical.
Here is a side-by-side comparison. First, read middle C as it appears in the treble clef, then in the bass clef. Both mean: press the same key in the middle of your piano.

blocks.caption: Middle C on the treble clef. It sits on a short line just below the stave, called a ledger line.
Middle C written in the bass clef. It sits on a short line just above the top line of the stave. That short line is called a ledger line.

blocks.label: Middle C, heard once, the same pitch in both clefs

blocks.md: One key. One pitch. Two different ways of writing it down. That is the power of middle C: it is the note that connects the treble world and the bass world.

Sit at your piano. Find and play middle C. Say the name out loud as you press the key. Then try playing the notes just above it (D4, E4) and just below it (B3, A3) to get a feel for where middle C lives.
Middle C is your home base. Whenever you feel lost on the keyboard, find middle C first and navigate from there. Nearly everything you learn in the early lessons will refer back to it.

items.prompt: Where does middle C sit in relation to the treble clef stave?
items.explain: Middle C falls below the five main lines of the treble clef. It sits on its own short ledger line directly underneath the stave.
options: On the middle line of the stave
On a ledger line just below the stave
On a ledger line just above the stave
On the bottom line of the stave

items.prompt: Middle C written in the treble clef and middle C written in the bass clef are the same key on the piano, producing the same pitch.
items.explain: Correct. The notation looks different because the two clefs have different frames of reference, but both symbols point to the exact same key in the middle of the keyboard.

items.prompt: What is a ledger line?
items.explain: A ledger line is a small extension of the stave, added only where needed, so that notes above or below the five main lines still have a clear position to sit on or between.
options: Another name for the bass clef symbol
The bottom line of the treble clef stave
A short extra line added above or below a stave for a note that falls outside the five main lines
A line that separates one bar from another

blocks.text: Putting It All Together: The Grand Stave

blocks.md:
You have now met the treble clef and the bass clef separately. In real piano music, both staves appear together. When they are joined, we call the result the **grand stave** (sometimes called the great stave).

A stave, remember, is the set of five horizontal lines on which music is written. The grand stave is simply two of those five-line staves placed one above the other, connected on the left side by a long vertical line and a square bracket. That bracket is a signal that the two staves belong together and are played by the same person, on the same instrument.

blocks.abc:
X:1
L:1/4
K:C
%%score {T B}
V:T clef=treble name="" subname=""
V:B clef=bass name="" subname=""
[V:T] E4
[V:B] G,4
blocks.caption: The grand stave. The treble clef stave sits on top; the bass clef stave sits below. Both are joined by a vertical line and bracket on the left. Right-hand notes appear on the top stave; left-hand notes appear on the bottom stave.

blocks.md:
Here is how the two staves divide the work between your hands:

- The **treble clef stave** (top) is read by your **right hand**.
- The **bass clef stave** (bottom) is read by your **left hand**.

This split is not a strict rule of nature. It is simply the way piano music is almost always written, and it is the convention you will see in every piece of sheet music you pick up.

**Grand stave = treble stave on top + bass stave below, joined by a bracket and a vertical line on the left.**
Right hand reads the top. Left hand reads the bottom.
Let's see the full range of note names across both staves together. Start at the bottom of the bass clef and work your way up through the treble clef. Each note is one step higher than the last.

blocks.abc:
X:1
L:1/4
K:C
%%score { (Treble) | (Bass) }
V:Treble clef=treble
V:Bass clef=bass
[V:Treble] x4 x4 x2 C D E F G A B c d e f
[V:Bass] G,, A,, B,, C, D, E, F, G, A, B, C x4 x4 x2
blocks.caption: The grand stave joins a treble clef (upper stave, higher notes) and a bass clef (lower stave, lower notes) with a brace and a bar line. White-note pitches climb from the low G of the bass clef up through middle C (the note on a short ledger line between the two staves, shown in both voices at the same position) to the upper notes of the treble clef.

blocks.md: When you sit at the piano, middle C is roughly in front of your body, slightly to the left of centre on a full-size keyboard. Use it as your landmark. Everything in the bass clef lives to the left of it; everything in the treble clef lives to the right.

blocks.label: Middle C on the keyboard, sitting between the ranges of the two staves

blocks.md:
Suppose you see a note sitting on the **second line from the bottom of the treble clef stave**.

1. Ask: which stave is it on? It is on the treble clef stave, so the right hand plays it.
2. Recall the lines of the treble clef  using the landmark system or a mnemonic.
3. The second line from the bottom is **G**.
4. Find G above middle C on the keyboard and play it with your right hand.

Now try the same process for any note you see on the bass clef stave
blocks.title: Reading a note on the grand stave: step by step

blocks.md:
Sit at the piano and try this three-step activity.

1. Play middle C with your right-hand thumb. Now play it with your left-hand thumb. It is the same key: the note that sits between the two staves.
2. Starting from middle C, play the next four white notes going up (D, E, F, G) with your right hand, one at a time. These are all treble clef notes.
3. Starting from middle C, play the next four white notes going down (B, A, G, F) with your left hand, one at a time. These are all bass clef notes.

Say the note name out loud as you play each one. There is no rush. Slow and accurate is exactly right at this stage.

items.prompt: What is the grand stave?
items.explain: The grand stave is two five-line staves, the treble clef on top and the bass clef below, connected by a vertical line and a bracket on the left. Together they give the full range needed for piano music.
options: A single stave with ten lines instead of five
The treble clef stave and the bass clef stave joined together
A stave used only for guitar music
Another name for the treble clef

items.prompt: When you read piano music from a grand stave, which stave does your left hand usually follow?
items.explain: By convention, the left hand reads the bass clef stave, which is the lower of the two staves on a grand stave. The right hand reads the treble clef stave on top.
options: Whichever stave has the louder notes
Both staves equally, with no fixed rule

items.prompt: Middle C is written on a short extra line between the two staves. What is that short extra line called?
items.explain: A ledger line is a small line added above or below a stave for notes that fall outside the five main lines. Middle C sits on its own ledger line between the treble and bass clef staves.

blocks.title: Check your understanding: The Grand Stave

blocks.md: Every piece of printed piano music you will ever play uses exactly what you have just learned. The right hand reads notes written on the treble clef stave. The left hand reads notes written on the bass clef stave. Together, those two staves form the grand stave, and it sits at the top of every page of piano sheet music. The next time you open a piece of music, even just to look at it, you can now name the clef on each stave, find Middle C sitting on its short ledger line between them, and read the names of the notes nearest to it.

- **Stave**: the set of five horizontal lines on which music is written
- **Line note**: a note whose oval head sits directly on one of the five lines
- **Space note**: a note whose oval head sits in the gap between two lines
- **Clef**: a symbol at the start of a stave that tells you the name of every line and space
- **Treble clef**: the clef used for higher-pitched notes, read mainly by the right hand at the piano
- **Bass clef**: the clef used for lower-pitched notes, read mainly by the left hand at the piano
- **Middle C**: the C note found near the middle of the piano keyboard, written on a short ledger line between the treble and bass staves
- **Ledger line**: a short extra line added above or below a stave to write notes that go beyond the five main lines
- **Grand stave**: the two staves joined together (treble on top, bass below) used for piano music

- A stave has five lines and four spaces. Notes sit on the lines or in the spaces.
- The treble clef marks the higher stave. Its line and space notes from bottom to top are E F G A B C D E F.
- The bass clef marks the lower stave. Its line and space notes from bottom to top are G A B C D E F G A.
- Middle C sits between the two staves on its own short ledger line. It is the landmark that links both clefs.
- The grand stave combines both staves and is the standard layout for all piano music.

items.prompt: A stave is made up of how many lines?
items.explain: A stave always has exactly five horizontal lines. Notes sit on the lines or in the spaces between them.

items.prompt: The treble clef curls around the second line from the bottom of the stave, fixing that line as which note?
items.explain: The treble clef is also called the G clef because its curl wraps around the second line, telling us that line is G above middle C (G4).

items.prompt: In the bass clef, which note sits on the middle (third) line of the stave?
items.explain: The lines of the bass clef from bottom to top are G, B, D, F, A. The middle (third) line is D.

items.prompt: Middle C sits on a short extra line called a ledger line, placed just below the treble clef stave and just above the bass clef stave.
items.explain: Middle C does not fit on either stave's five lines, so it is written on its own small ledger line between the two staves. This is what makes it the joining note of the grand stave.

items.prompt: The grand stave joins the treble clef stave and the bass clef stave together. Which instrument most commonly reads from a grand stave?
items.explain: The piano uses both hands at once, one reading the treble clef (usually the right hand) and one reading the bass clef (usually the left hand). The grand stave shows both together.
